overall_summary: Analysis of deduplicated YouTube Shorts performance indicates clear audience preference for space-based 'What If' scenarios and extreme planetary phenomena. Videos featuring hypothetical catastrophic scenarios or bizarre space mechanics (e.g., liquid diamond planets, falling into extreme environments, and dark planets) generated significantly higher views-per-day and like-to-view ratios compared to standard static facts or historical/psychological trivia.

winning_patterns.evidence: Videos like 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (1,024 views) and 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (972 views) vastly outperform static fact formats published in the same window.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on 'What If' scenarios applied to extreme astrophysical bodies, focusing on immersive survival physics.

winning_patterns.evidence: Titles detailing surreal planetary conditions ('The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b', 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!') drive high engagement and strong like ratios.
winning_patterns.action: Continue producing ultra-niche space anomalies framed around sensory extremes (sight, sound, pressure, touch).

weak_patterns.evidence: Topics like song memory loops and fake memories ('Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories') stalled under 100 views with negligible engagement.
weak_patterns.action: Deprioritize psychology facts and cognitive illusions unless reframed into high-stakes hypothetical survival or mystery narratives.

weak_patterns.evidence: General historical mysteries ('The 2,000-Year-Old Mystery Science Can't Solve') and deep ocean facts failed to gain traction relative to space content.
weak_patterns.action: Shift away from standard historical trivia and redirect narrative energy into the newly introduced cinematic storytelling and micro-drama niches.
